import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 5.54

by J. Wiegold

Let $p, q, r$ be distinct primes and $u(x, y, z)$ a commutator word in three
variables. Prove that there exist (infinitely many?) natural numbers $n$ such
that the alternating group $\mathbb{A}_n$ can be generated by three elements
$\xi, \eta, \zeta$ satisfying
$\xi^p = \eta^q = \zeta^r = \xi \eta \zeta \cdot u(\xi, \eta, \zeta) = 1$.

Here a commutator word in three variables is an element $u$ of the derived
subgroup of the free group on $x, y, z$, and $u(\xi, \eta, \zeta)$ is the value
of $u$ at $\xi, \eta, \zeta$, i.e. the image of $u$ under the homomorphism
sending $x, y, z$ to $\xi, \eta, \zeta$. The free group on $x, y, z$ is modelled
as `FreeGroup (Fin 3)`, with $x, y, z$ the generators indexed by $0, 1, 2$.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«5.54»

/--
Let $p, q, r$ be distinct primes and $u(x, y, z)$ a commutator word in three
variables, i.e. an element of the derived subgroup of the free group on
$x, y, z$. Then there exists a natural number $n$ such that the alternating
group $\mathbb{A}_n$ can be generated by three elements $\xi, \eta, \zeta$
satisfying $\xi^p = \eta^q = \zeta^r = \xi \eta \zeta \cdot u(\xi, \eta, \zeta) = 1$.

The condition $n \geq 3$ only excludes the trivial groups $\mathbb{A}_0$,
$\mathbb{A}_1$, $\mathbb{A}_2$, for which $\xi = \eta = \zeta = 1$ is a
degenerate witness.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«5.54» (p q r : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime) (hr : r.Prime)
    (hpq : p ≠ q) (hpr : p ≠ r) (hqr : q ≠ r)
    (u : FreeGroup (Fin 3)) (hu : u ∈ commutator (FreeGroup (Fin 3))) :
    ∃ n : ℕ, 3 ≤ n ∧ ∃ ξ η ζ : alternatingGroup (Fin n),
      Subgroup.closure {ξ, η, ζ} = ⊤ ∧
      ξ ^ p = 1 ∧ η ^ q = 1 ∧ ζ ^ r = 1 ∧
      ξ * η * ζ * FreeGroup.lift ![ξ, η, ζ] u = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
Let $p, q, r$ be distinct primes and $u(x, y, z)$ a commutator word in three
variables, i.e. an element of the derived subgroup of the free group on
$x, y, z$. Are there infinitely many natural numbers $n$ such that the
alternating group $\mathbb{A}_n$ can be generated by three elements
$\xi, \eta, \zeta$ satisfying
$\xi^p = \eta^q = \zeta^r = \xi \eta \zeta \cdot u(\xi, \eta, \zeta) = 1$?

The question asks whether this holds for all such $p, q, r$ and $u$. No lower bound
on $n$ is needed here: the trivial groups $\mathbb{A}_n$, $n \leq 2$, contribute
only finitely many degenerate witnesses.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«5.54».variants.infinitely_many : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ (p q r : ℕ), p.Prime → q.Prime → r.Prime → p ≠ q → p ≠ r → q ≠ r →
    ∀ u ∈ commutator (FreeGroup (Fin 3)),
      {n : ℕ | ∃ ξ η ζ : alternatingGroup (Fin n),
        Subgroup.closure {ξ, η, ζ} = ⊤ ∧
        ξ ^ p = 1 ∧ η ^ q = 1 ∧ ζ ^ r = 1 ∧
        ξ * η * ζ * FreeGroup.lift ![ξ, η, ζ] u = 1}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«5.54»

This makes the literal infinitely-many variant negatively answered by a degenerate case; I followed the literal statement and flagged this in modeling_decisions.
modeling_decisions: "Commutator word in three variables" is read as an element of the derived subgroup of the free group on x,y,z, i.e. `u ∈ commutator (FreeGroup (Fin 3))` (the reading the decomposition table calls primary). The narrower reading (a single commutator [v,w]) is a special case; since u is universally quantified, the chosen reading is at least as strong.

This reading includes the trivial word u = 1 (as would any reading via single commutators [v,w], taking v = w). For (p,q,r) = (2,3,5) and u = 1 the relations define the triangle group Δ(2,3,5) ≅ A_5, so the only witnesses are n ∈ {0,1,2,5}; hence, read literally, the infinitely-many variant is answered negatively by this degenerate instance. The source does not state u ≠ 1, so the literal statement was kept; a reviewer may wish to consider whether Wiegold intended u to be non-trivial (adding `u ≠ 1` to the variant).
u(ξ,η,ζ) is `FreeGroup.lift ![ξ, η, ζ] u`, with x,y,z the generators indexed 0,1,2 (checked: `of 0 ↦ ξ`, `of 1 ↦ η`, `of 2 ↦ ζ`).

Degenerate witnesses: A_n is trivial for n ≤ 2 and then ξ=η=ζ=1 satisfies every relation (verified in Lean for n = 2). The primary slot requires 3 ≤ n, which excludes exactly these. A_3 (cyclic of order 3, where u evaluates to 1 and at most one of p,q,r equals 3) and A_4 (where u evaluates into V_4 while ξηζ lies in a coset of 3-cycles) can never be witnesses, so 3 ≤ n is equivalent to the alternative 5 ≤ n suggested in the table; the minimal exclusion was chosen. The relations were kept literal (ξ^p = 1 etc.) rather than requiring orders exactly p,q,r, since the latter would change the statement for elements ξ = 1.
The variant `(infinitely many?)` is posed as a question, so it uses `answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ p q r u, Set.Infinite {n | …}` with all quantifiers after `answer(sorry)`; no lower bound on n is needed there.
Distinctness of the primes is expressed as p ≠ q, p ≠ r, q ≠ r; primality via `Nat.Prime`.

by J. Wiegold

variables. Prove that there exist (infinitely many?) natural numbers $n$ such
that the alternating group $\mathbb{A}_n$ can be generated by three elements
$\xi, \eta, \zeta$ satisfying
$\xi^p = \eta^q = \zeta^r = \xi \eta \zeta \cdot u(\xi, \eta, \zeta) = 1$.

A commutator word in the variables $x, y, z$ is an element of the derived
subgroup $F' = [F, F]$ of the free group $F = F(x, y, z)$; here $F$ is
`FreeGroup (Fin 3)` with $x, y, z$ the generators `0, 1, 2`, and
$u(\xi, \eta, \zeta)$ is the image of $u$ under the homomorphism

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)

namespace Kourovka.«5.54»

/--
`IsWiegoldGenerated p q r u n` says that the alternating group $\mathbb{A}_n$
(realised as `alternatingGroup (Fin n)`) is generated by three elements
$\xi, \eta, \zeta$ satisfying
$\xi^p = \eta^q = \zeta^r = \xi \eta \zeta \cdot u(\xi, \eta, \zeta) = 1$,
where $u(\xi, \eta, \zeta)$ is the image of the word `u : FreeGroup (Fin 3)`
under the homomorphism sending the generators `0, 1, 2` to $\xi, \eta, \zeta$.
-/
def IsWiegoldGenerated (p q r : ℕ) (u : FreeGroup (Fin 3)) (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ ξ η ζ : alternatingGroup (Fin n),
    Subgroup.closure {ξ, η, ζ} = ⊤ ∧
      ξ ^ p = 1 ∧ η ^ q = 1 ∧ ζ ^ r = 1 ∧ ξ * η * ζ * FreeGroup.lift ![ξ, η, ζ] u = 1

/-- The trivial group $\mathbb{A}_0$ is a degenerate witness for every $p, q, r$ and $u$:
take $\xi = \eta = \zeta = 1$. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem isWiegoldGenerated_zero (p q r : ℕ) (u : FreeGroup (Fin 3)) :
    IsWiegoldGenerated p q r u 0 :=
  ⟨1, 1, 1, Subsingleton.elim _ _, one_pow _, one_pow _, one_pow _, Subsingleton.elim _ _⟩

/--
Let $p, q, r$ be distinct primes and $u(x, y, z)$ a commutator word in three
variables, i.e. an element of the derived subgroup of the free group on
$x, y, z$. Then there exists a natural number $n$ such that the alternating
group $\mathbb{A}_n$ can be generated by three elements $\xi, \eta, \zeta$
satisfying $\xi^p = \eta^q = \zeta^r = \xi \eta \zeta \cdot u(\xi, \eta, \zeta) = 1$.

which $\mathbb{A}_n$ is trivial and $\xi = \eta = \zeta = 1$ satisfies every
relation. (For $n = 3, 4$ no such generating triple exists, since $p, q, r$ are
distinct primes, so the restriction loses nothing.)
-/

    (hpq : p ≠ q) (hpr : p ≠ r) (hqr : q ≠ r)
    (u : FreeGroup (Fin 3)) (hu : u ∈ commutator (FreeGroup (Fin 3))) :
    ∃ n, 5 ≤ n ∧ IsWiegoldGenerated p q r u n := by
  sorry

/--
